strengths: The core motivation of augmenting Minimum Weight Perfect Matching (MWPM) with dynamic, data-driven edge weights to better capture correlated noise (such as depolarizing noise) is sound and addresses a well-recognized limitation of standard independent-noise matching.

The hybrid architecture effectively combines localized graph convolutions (TransformerConv) with an edge-level Transformer encoder to capture both local syndrome geometry and long-range defect interactions.

Empirical results on both the periodic Toric code (distances 6, 8, 10) and rotated surface code (distances 5, 7) show reductions in logical error rate (LER) compared to standard MWPM, BPOSD-2, and QECCT under depolarizing noise.
The paper maintains a relatively compact and parameter-efficient model footprint (~3.9M parameters) across the tested lattice sizes.
weaknesses: Misleading characterization of differentiability and end-to-end optimization: The manuscript repeatedly claims to introduce a 'differentiable decoding framework' and a 'proxy loss function that enables end-to-end optimization' through the non-differentiable MWPM algorithm. In reality, the training is standard supervised binary cross-entropy on heuristic edge labels plus an entropy regularizer. The MWPM algorithm is completely decoupled from the training pipeline and only executed post-hoc at inference time.

Suboptimal handling of quantum degeneracy: Topological codes exhibit massive degeneracy, where many distinct physical error chains belong to the same logical equivalence class. Supervised edge classification against an arbitrarily selected ground-truth matching penalizes the model for predicting equally valid homologous chains. The heuristic clustering and brute-force approach (Algorithm 2) does not address this fundamental ambiguity, which can destabilize training or bias predicted edge weights.

Prohibitive computational complexity and absence of latency benchmarking: The architecture feeds all edges of the complete defect graph into a Transformer encoder, yielding a complexity of O(|E|^2 d_{hidden}) = O(|V|^4 d_{hidden}). In fault-tolerant quantum computing, real-time decoding requires sub-microsecond latencies. The paper does not report any runtime, wall-clock decoding time, or hardware latency comparisons against fast decoders like Fusion Blossom or PyMatching.

Lack of statistical rigor and error bars: In Figures 2, 3, and 4, logical error rates and threshold estimates (e.g., 17.9% and 10.95%) are reported without confidence intervals, standard errors, or formal finite-size scaling fits.

Minor presentation issues: In Figure 3(a), the legend contains a typo ('NNWPM' instead of 'NMWPM'), and several diagrams in Figure 1 and Figure 7 have awkward overlapping labels or low-contrast rendering.

strengths: Principled hybrid formulation: Augmenting MWPM with learned dynamic edge weights combines the inductive bias of graph/attention architectures with the structural guarantees of classical matching algorithms, ensuring that the decoder always produces a valid matching.

Comprehensive empirical benchmarking: The authors evaluate their method on both Toric and Rotated Surface codes under independent and depolarizing noise models, benchmarking against relevant baselines including standard MWPM (PyMatching), BPOSD-2, and QECCT.

Well-structured architectural description: The manuscript provides detailed architectural specifications and clear schematic diagrams (Figures 1, 6, and 7) explaining node/edge feature construction and the combination of local GNN layers with a Transformer encoder.
weaknesses: Misleading characterization of 'end-to-end differentiable optimization': The paper repeatedly claims to solve the non-differentiability barrier of MWPM by formulating a 'novel proxy loss function that enables end-to-end optimization' through the matching algorithm. In reality, the network is trained via standard supervised learning (binary cross-entropy with entropy regularization) against precomputed heuristic edge labels (Algorithm 2). MWPM is simply executed post-hoc at inference time, meaning there is no gradient flow, differentiable relaxation, or end-to-end optimization through the matching step.

Neglect of quantum degeneracy in the supervised objective: In topological QEC, decoding requires identifying the correct homology class rather than a unique physical error string; many distinct matchings differ only by stabilizer loops and are equally valid. By training with binary cross-entropy against a single heuristic matching chosen by Algorithm 2, the loss penalizes alternative valid matchings in the same equivalence class, which is a known limitation of direct edge-supervised learning for degenerate quantum codes.

Unfavorable computational scaling and absence of latency benchmarks: The Transformer encoder operates on all edges of the defect graph, yielding $O(|E|^2) = O(|V|^4)$ complexity in the number of defects. Given that real-time fault-tolerant QEC requires decoding latencies on the order of microseconds per syndrome cycle, this dense attention overhead is a major practical concern. The paper does not provide empirical runtime comparisons or wall-clock decoding throughput against PyMatching or Fusion Blossom.

Limited noise realism and code sizes: The experimental evaluation is restricted to code-capacity noise (perfect syndrome measurements) on small lattices (Toric code up to $L=10$, Rotated Surface code only up to $L=7$). Real fault-tolerant implementations operate under circuit-level phenomenological noise with measurement errors across 3D space-time graphs, where scaling and performance characteristics can differ significantly.

strengths: Compelling motivation: Enhancing MWPM with learned, syndrome-dependent dynamic edge weights is a principled hybrid strategy that preserves the topological validity guarantees of classical matching while enabling sensitivity to correlated errors (e.g., depolarizing noise where $Y = iXZ$ creates correlations between $X$ and $Z$ syndromes).

Promising logical error rate reductions: The empirical results demonstrate clear improvements in Logical Error Rate (LER) and threshold over standard static MWPM and BPOSD-2 baselines under depolarizing noise for Toric and Rotated Surface codes.
Clear architectural description: The paper provides clear mathematical definitions of node and edge feature encodings, the GNN backbone, and the preprocessing transformations.
weaknesses: Misleading claims regarding differentiability and end-to-end optimization: The paper repeatedly claims to propose a 'differentiable decoding framework' that enables 'end-to-end optimization' and 'training through the non-differentiable MWPM algorithm' via a proxy loss. In reality, the network is trained strictly via supervised learning (binary cross-entropy + entropy regularization) against target edge labels generated offline by an algorithmic clustering heuristic (Algorithm 2). MWPM is entirely absent from the training loop, and no gradients flow through or approximate the matching operator.

Fundamental tension with quantum degeneracy: Quantum codes are degenerate, meaning many distinct physical error chains generate identical syndromes and belong to the same logical equivalence class. Supervised edge classification against a single heuristic target matching penalizes valid alternative matchings within the same homology class, an issue that is neither addressed nor analyzed in the loss formulation.

Prohibitive computational complexity and lack of runtime analysis: The model constructs a complete graph over active defects and feeds all $E = \Theta(|V|^2)$ edges as tokens into a Transformer encoder. This results in dense self-attention scaling as $O(E^2) = O(|V|^4)$ with respect to the defect count. Real-time fault-tolerant decoding (e.g., in superconducting architectures) requires microsecond-scale latency. The manuscript provides no wall-clock inference times, latency benchmarks, or throughput comparisons against fast decoders like PyMatching or Fusion Blossom.

Absence of ablation studies: The paper lacks essential ablations isolating the contribution of its core components, such as removing the Transformer encoder (GNN-only), removing the GNN (Transformer-only), or evaluating the sensitivity to the entropy regularization weight $\lambda$ (including $\lambda = 0$).

Restricted noise regime and missing experimental rigor: The evaluation is limited strictly to code capacity noise on small lattices ($L \le 10$ for Toric, $L \le 7$ for Surface code) without syndrome measurement errors or circuit-level noise, which requires 3D spacetime decoding graphs. Furthermore, Figures 2–4 lack error bars, confidence intervals, and information on the number of Monte Carlo sample shots used.

strengths: Sound hybrid design: Combining geometric deep learning (GNN + Transformer) with classical MWPM ensures that the decoder always produces valid topological corrections while learning data-dependent edge weights that capture correlations (e.g., Y-errors under depolarizing noise) that standard MWPM struggles with.

Strong empirical threshold performance: The method achieves impressive depolarizing noise thresholds (17.9% on Toric code and 17.7% on Rotated Surface code), which approach the maximum likelihood theoretical limits and convincingly outperform classical MWPM baselines and competitive neural decoders like QECCT.

Parameter scalability: Unlike models whose parameter counts scale quadratically or linearly with lattice dimensions (such as QECCT, which swells to >6.6M params at distance 10), NMWPM maintains a virtually constant footprint of ~4.0M parameters across evaluated code distances.

Thorough ablation and runtime analysis: The paper includes meaningful ablations (verifying the contribution of entropy regularization, geometric embeddings, and edge features) alongside an inference latency comparison on an NVIDIA L40 GPU.
weaknesses: Misleading characterization of 'differentiable training / end-to-end optimization': The paper repeatedly states (in the Abstract, Introduction, and Contributions) that it formulates a proxy loss to enable 'end-to-end optimization' through the non-differentiable MWPM algorithm. In reality, the training pipeline does not backpropagate through MWPM or a continuous relaxation thereof; rather, it performs supervised edge-label classification using BCE and entropy regularization against offline pseudo-ground-truth edge matchings. This should be accurately framed as supervised edge-weight learning rather than end-to-end learning through a combinatorial solver.

Scalability bottleneck of ground-truth label generation: The supervised target labels rely on Algorithm 2 (clustering and localized MWPM with brute-force permutation fallback when logical errors occur). Because it requires explicit knowledge of the simulated physical error configuration and incurs fallback search overhead (even with a 10s timeout), scaling ground-truth label generation to larger distances ($L > 12$) or complex fault-tolerant circuit models becomes a serious bottleneck.

Computational scaling of the edge Transformer: The edge processing block applies a dense Transformer encoder over all edges $E$ in the defect graph, resulting in $O(E^2) = O(|V|^4)$ complexity in terms of defect count $|V|$. While manageable for small distances, this quaternary defect scaling could be prohibitive in large-scale fault-tolerant regimes with dense syndrome defects.

Limited evaluation on realistic circuit-level noise: The primary results are on code capacity phenomenological noise (Toric and Rotated planar). Circuit-level noise benchmarks are relegated to an appendix and restricted to very small distances ($L=3, 5$ repetition code and $L=3$ rotated planar code), leaving open how well the architecture scales to 3D spacetime matching graphs.

strengths: The hybrid paradigm—leveraging deep neural networks to dynamically predict edge weights that feed into a classical, structurally guaranteed MWPM solver—is an intuitive and promising direction for incorporating correlated noise into topological quantum decoders.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning multiple code families (toric, rotated surface, and repetition codes) and noise models (independent, depolarizing, and circuit-level noise), with reported thresholds close to maximum-likelihood limits.
Good set of ablation experiments (testing geometric embeddings, edge features, entropy regularization, and pooling choices) and transfer learning experiments across code distances.
weaknesses: Misleading characterization of the optimization framework: The paper repeatedly claims to provide a 'novel proxy loss function that enables end-to-end optimization' through the non-differentiable MWPM algorithm. In reality, MWPM is never in the training loop; the network is trained via standard supervised edge classification (BCE + entropy penalty) against pseudo-ground-truth edge labels generated offline by Algorithm 2. This is decoupled supervised learning, not end-to-end differentiation through combinatorial matching.

Neglect of quantum degeneracy during supervised training: Quantum error correction relies on identifying the correct homological equivalence class, not a unique physical error string. Algorithm 2 deterministically selects a single matching as the 'ground truth' and penalizes any alternative valid matching via binary cross-entropy, even if that alternative produces the identical logical outcome. This introduces artificial label noise and suboptimality.

Severe computational scalability bottleneck: The Transformer Encoder operates over all $E$ edges in the defect graph. For a complete graph on $|V|$ syndrome defects, $E = O(|V|^2)$, meaning the self-attention over edges scales as $O(E^2) = O(|V|^4) = O(L^8)$ in the worst case. This extreme complexity limits the approach to small lattice sizes ($L \le 12$) and results in millisecond-scale latency (Table 6 reports ~4 ms on an L40 GPU), which is several orders of magnitude too slow for real-time fault-tolerant hardware cycles (~microsecond regime).

Missing error bars and statistical rigor for threshold estimation: The threshold differences claimed over baselines (e.g., 17.9% vs. 17.8% for QECCT in Toric depolarizing noise) are tiny, yet the threshold curves in Figure 2 lack Monte Carlo error bars, confidence intervals, and details on the number of sampled shots per point. Additionally, Table 5 labels the threshold column with '(\downarrow)', which incorrectly implies lower is better for error thresholds.

strengths: Sound hybrid design: Combining geometric deep learning with classical Minimum Weight Perfect Matching (MWPM) leverages the expressiveness of neural networks to handle correlated Pauli errors while retaining the guaranteed structural validity and polynomial solvability of matching algorithms.

Strong empirical threshold results: On the toric code under depolarizing noise, NMWPM achieves a threshold of 17.9% (approaching the 18.9% maximum-likelihood limit) and 10.95% under independent noise (near the 11.0% limit), outperforming standard MWPM and competitive recent baselines such as QECCT and BPOSD-2.

Constant parameter count across code distances: Unlike baselines such as QECCT where the parameter count scales noticeably with code distance, NMWPM maintains an approximately constant parameter footprint (~4M parameters) across distances L=6 to L=10.

Informative ablation and analysis: The paper includes useful ablation experiments analyzing the role of entropy regularization, feature encodings, edge aggregation strategies, and cross-code-distance transfer learning.
weaknesses: Overstated claim regarding end-to-end optimization through non-differentiable MWPM: The paper repeatedly claims to provide an 'end-to-end optimization' that circumvents or trains through the non-differentiable MWPM algorithm. In practice, the training pipeline is standard supervised binary edge classification against ground-truth labels produced by an offline heuristic (Algorithm 2). The classical MWPM algorithm is not differentiated through, nor is it part of the backward computational graph.

High computational scaling of the edge Transformer: The architecture applies a Transformer Encoder treating every edge in the defect graph as a token. For |V| active defects, there are E = O(|V|^2) edges, resulting in an attention complexity of O(E^2) = O(|V|^4). Because |V| scales with p * L^2, this scales as O(p^4 * L^8), presenting a severe computational bottleneck when scaling to larger lattice sizes (L >= 15) or fault-tolerant space-time graphs.

Limited evaluation on circuit-level noise: Practical quantum error correction must handle faulty syndrome measurements across repeated rounds in a 3D space-time graph. The manuscript focuses primarily on phenomenological/code-capacity noise, while circuit-level noise is only evaluated on tiny systems (repetition code L=3, 5 and rotated surface code L=3), leaving open how well the edge-transformer formulation scales to 3D space-time detector graphs.

Ambiguities in graph definition: Section 4.2 introduces the graph G=(V,E) where V is the set of active defects, but then describes node features and modulated syndrome embeddings computed over all N stabilizers in the code. It is not entirely clear whether the GNN operates on the full stabilizer lattice or only the active defect subgraph, and how the edge set passed to the Transformer is bounded.
